pages.title: Parenting Arrangements
pages.body: Parenting arrangements include where children live, day-to-day care, and decisions about school and healthcare after separation. Informal agreements, written parenting plans and court-made parenting orders have different legal effects. Sharing responsibility for some major decisions does not mean children must spend equal time with each parent. Where family violence is involved, direct negotiation may be unsafe.

pages.title: Contact with the Other Parent
pages.body: Separation does not automatically decide whether or when children spend time with the other parent. Arrangements need to consider their best interests, including safety, individual needs and views. Family violence may affect how contact is arranged; neither contact nor no contact can be assumed for every family. Any existing court orders need individual legal review.

Ask a legal service about its terms, proposed changes or possible breaches.

pages.title: Relocation with Children
pages.body: There is no single answer to whether a parent can move with children to another city. Relevant questions include existing parenting orders, how a move may affect time with the other parent or major decisions, school arrangements and family violence. Leaving a violent relationship does not mean court orders can be ignored. A partner’s statement is not a legal ruling, but it also does not establish that a move is legally permitted.

pages.title: AVOs and Parenting Orders

An AVO and parenting orders are different legal orders; an AVO does not automatically cancel all parenting arrangements. If their terms appear to conflict, a lawyer needs to consider the actual documents and applicable law. Seek individual advice about safety concerns during handovers or contact.

Changing settings can itself affect safety, so a generic account-reset checklist is not appropriate for every family.

Conditions include relationship status, principal carer responsibilities, the youngest child’s age, income, assets and residency. Age limits differ for single and partnered carers; check the current official eligibility rules. Separation does not automatically establish entitlement.

pages.title: Family Tax Benefit
pages.body: Family Tax Benefit has Part A and Part B and helps eligible families with the costs of raising children. Eligibility and payment amounts depend on factors including children’s ages, care percentages, income and other requirements. Separation or a change in care may require updated information. Services Australia can explain how child support may affect Family Tax Benefit.

pages.title: Child Support
pages.body: Child support concerns the financial costs of raising children after separation. Services Australia can explain assessments, collection and how care percentages may affect payments. Parenting orders and child support are different matters; contact arrangements alone do not establish a payment amount. Where seeking child support creates family violence concerns, ask Services Australia about possible Maintenance Action Test exemptions; approval requires assessment.

pages.title: Child Care Subsidy
pages.body: Child Care Subsidy helps eligible families pay for approved childcare. Conditions include the child’s age, approved care, fee liability and residency, along with other current program rules. Families experiencing violence and temporary financial hardship can also ask about Additional Child Care Subsidy. Further eligibility assessment is required; this site cannot approve support.

pages.title: Crisis & Leaving Violence Payments
pages.body: Crisis Payment and the Leaving Violence Program are separate programs. Crisis Payment has requirements for eligible extreme circumstances and severe financial hardship. The Leaving Violence Program provides financial and other support to eligible people experiencing intimate partner violence who are planning or have made a change in living arrangements. Each has its own application rules; leaving a relationship does not automatically qualify a person.

pages.title: Financial Safety
pages.body: Financial abuse can involve restricting access to money, preventing work, creating debt, controlling online accounts or continuing financial pressure after separation. Official information and specialist services can help explain options. Child support, bank accounts and shared devices may create connected safety concerns. Individual professional advice is preferable to a universal set of account-changing instructions.
